transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-15
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (VentureBank Head of AI), Mark Dawson (Infra Lead), Lydia Chen (CISO), Tom Rivera (PM)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand VentureBank's inference needs, preference for dedicated/reserved GPUs for latency and data isolation, burst handling and scaling expectations, and security/compliance constraints. Agreement to run a short pilot on Dedicated capacity and share benchmarks and pricing.

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Traffic profile and latency SLOs
- Isolation (data residency, PCI/SOC2 concerns)
- Burst strategy and autoscaling behavior
- Model types and memory/kv cache characteristics
- Pricing/commit considerations and pilot next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, joined by Maya our systems SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Sara: Doing well, thanks. Appreciate you fitting this in. We wanted to cover dedicated capacity options, isolation, and how you handle bursts.
[00:10] Maya: Great. High level, we'll ask about your current infra, traffic patterns, SLOs, and security requirements. Then we can map that to Dedicated sizing, burst lanes, and private deployment options.
[00:18] Tom: Sounds good. I'll jump in on product needs; Sara will cover models and ML specifics, Mark on infra.
[00:24] Sara: Quick background: VentureBank runs several generative AI features in our customer support product — triage, response drafting, and some smart-case summarization. We use a mix of open and fine-tuned ~7B and 13B models, some Llama-derived, some in-house fine-tunes. Latency target is p95 under 300ms for single-turn generation for UI flows; for longer summarizations we're OK with 1.5-2s.
[00:44] Maya: Helpful. Are you on hosted endpoints today or self-hosted?
[00:47] Mark: We're mostly on AWS EKS with model endpoints on EC2/GPU instances. For experiments we test on SageMaker, but production has been pretty manual scaling, which is hitting ops limits. We want predictable throughput for peak business hours and strict isolation for PII and PCI scopes.
[01:05] Alex: Understood. So Dedicated makes sense — reserved GPU pools give you predictable throughput and isolation. Quick question: what's your typical and peak RPS for the generation workloads?
[01:14] Mark: Typical is around 25 RPS across all services, peaks up to 180 RPS for short bursts during business hours. The burst often lasts 5-10 minutes, but there are occasionally sustained high periods for 30-45 minutes.
[01:28] Maya: Ok that burst profile is common. We support a burst queue and can provision additional capacity for bursts — either via warm standby or autoscaling pools. The warm standby gives faster cold-start behavior because weights are preloaded into GPU memory.
[01:40] Sara: Curious about cost tradeoffs — is warm standby much more expensive than pure autoscaling?
[01:44] Alex: There is a premium for reserved standby, but it's predictable. The autoscaling model is more cost-efficient but adds some variance in tail latency during heavy bursts. We usually recommend a hybrid: baseline reserved for your steady-state and a burst pool configured with quick spin-up for those short peaks.
[01:58] Tom: For privacy/regulatory reasons we need network isolation and dedicated tenancy, not just logical separation. Does Redwood Dedicated provide VPC peering or private link and also an option for on-prem or VPC private deployment?
[02:11] Maya: Yes — Dedicated supports private network connectivity via VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink. For customers with strict requirements we also offer Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) where the control plane is customer-managed.
[02:23] Lydia: Security — we need SOC 2 compliance, audit logs, KMS integration for key management, and support for customer-managed keys. Also data retention policies: we need to ensure no customer data is persisted outside our control.
[02:36] Alex: We can provide SOC 2 docs, audit log exports, and KMS/HSM integrations. For Dedicated, logs and data residency are configurable; we can support locking down logs to your S3 and ensure no training data retention. We'll share the security pack after the call.
[02:50] Mark: On the model side, we're using KV cache heavily for long context summarization. Does Redwood Dedicated preserve KV across requests for the same session?
[02:58] Maya: We support KV cache management and session affinity; you can pin sessions to instances to reuse KV cache, which reduces tokens and latency for long conversations. We do caveat about memory footprint — for 13B models with long context, you'll want H100-style memory or aggressive quantization.
[03:15] Sara: That brings up quantization — what do you support? We're exploring int8 and some 4-bit approaches to lower GPU memory.
[03:21] Maya: We support quantized variants and can recommend model/quantization pairings. For production we often benchmark both int8 and 4-bit quantizations, and sometimes a mixed approach where high-priority requests run on fp16/higher precision and lower-priority run on quantized variants.
[03:33] Tom: For the pilot, we'd want to validate latency at our traffic shape and cost per 1M tokens. How fast can we run benchmarks?
[03:39] Alex: We can spin up a pilot cluster on Dedicated in a couple days after contract/po — for a proof-of-concept we usually do a 2-week pilot: first week ingest traffic profile and run baseline benchmarks, second week tune batching, caching and autoscaling. Maya: We'll provide the benchmark template and can help interpret results.
[03:55] Mark: On autoscaling — are you doing GPU autoscaling (spin up new instances) or RPC-level routing? How do you avoid cold-start latency?
[04:02] Maya: We do both. For Dedicated, the orchestration includes instance-level autoscaling and fast warm-pooling. We can also do request-level routing to standby model variants (lower cost) under heavy load. Cold-start is mitigated by pre-warmed pools and model layering.
[04:16] Sara: Any limitations on model licensing? We have some Llama-derived fine-tunes and one proprietary weight that we cannot allow outside our VPC.
[04:24] Alex: For proprietary weights we recommend Redwood Private or Dedicated with strict network isolation. You can bring-your-own-model (BYOM) and we won't persist the artifacts outside your control. We'll detail the BYOM process in the security pack.
[04:36] Lydia: On compliance, we need to know if audit trails meet our internal audit team requirements — specifically who accessed models, keys, and ability to revoke access quickly.
[04:45] Maya: Audit trails are per-request with identity info; RBAC integrates with SSO/SAML and we provide access revocation via IAM role mappings. We'll include sample audit outputs.
[04:54] Tom: Pricing question: do you charge per-GPU reserved plus a per-token runtime? Or is it combined?
[04:59] Alex: Typically Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract (monthly commit) priced by GPU type and node count, plus a small runtime/unit charge for extra usage — variable depending on model family and quantization. We'll send detailed tiers.
[05:12] Mark: For sizing, with our peak 180 RPS which includes many short single-turn requests, do you have a rule-of-thumb for GPUs per RPS for 7B and 13B models?
[05:21] Maya: Rough rule: a single A100 or H100 can serve roughly 60-120 RPS for optimized 7B models depending on batch sizing and prompt length; 13B drops that by ~30-50% depending on sequence length. But we strongly recommend running your actual traces through our benchmark to get accurate numbers.
[05:39] Sara: We need to keep UI latency p95 under 300ms. If we reserve for steady 30 RPS and burst to 180, what's the expected tail behavior?
[05:48] Maya: If the burst pool is properly warmed, p95 should hold within SLO. If relying solely on cold autoscaling, you will see degradation. For your profile we recommend baseline reservation for 30-40 RPS and a warm burst pool sized to handle 150 RPS with quick failover to a lower-cost variant if absolutely needed.
[06:05] Tom: Can we specify fallback policies — like route to a smaller quantized model if p95 goes above threshold?
[06:10] Alex: Yes, smart routing and automatic fallbacks are supported. You can configure routing by latency, cost, or region, and have automatic downgrade to a compatible quantized variant.
[06:18] Lydia: On data residency, our customers are US-only and we need all inference to remain in us-east-1. Does Dedicated allow region pinning?
[06:25] Maya: Absolutely. You can pin regions; Dedicated can be provisioned in a specific region and we can disable cross-region replication for that instance.
[06:32] Mark: Operationally, how do we monitor token usage and cost per route?
[06:36] Alex: Redwood Console provides per-route/model token breakdowns, tracing hooks, and cost attribution. We'll give you a demo of the console in the next call.
[06:45] Sara: For the pilot success criteria: 1) meet p95 < 300ms for UI flows under production traffic; 2) demonstrate encryption and KMS integration; 3) show cost per 1M tokens within target; 4) show plan for isolation and audit.
[06:58] Alex: That's fair. We'll commit to helping with benchmarks that map to those criteria.
[07:02] Tom: Any typical gotchas?
[07:04] Maya: Watch out for prompt length variance — longer context increases memory and reduces RPS. Also KV cache affinity needs careful session routing. And model warm-up — if you don't keep a warm pool, tail latency will spike.
[07:18] Sara: One more: how do you handle model rollouts and version pinning? We need canary and A/B tests.
[07:24] Alex: Redwood supports rollouts, canaries, and automatic fallback. You can pin versions and route percentage of traffic for A/B.
[07:31] Lydia: Ok, security follow-ups: we'll want SOC 2 artifacts and a short questionnaire answered. We'll send that to the contact on your side.
[07:38] Alex: Please send it to me and Maya and we'll loop in security if needed.
[07:42] Maya: We'll also prepare the benchmark template and a checklist for BYOM and private deployment.
[07:47] Tom: Timeline — assuming pricing looks OK, we're aiming for a pilot start in early May. Does that sound doable?
[07:53] Alex: Yes. We'll send pricing and benchmark docs by Friday (2026-04-17). If you provide traces and security questionnaire next week, we can spin up a pilot the week of May 4.
[08:03] Sara: Great.
[08:05] Alex: Any other questions?
[08:07] Lydia: Not right now.
[08:08] Mark: No.
[08:09] Tom: All good.
[08:10] Alex: Awesome. Recap of action items and next steps, then we'll close.
[08:14] Alex: Action items — Alex send pricing + tiers; Maya send benchmark + quantization notes; Mark upload traces; Lydia send security questionnaire. We'll schedule 1h deep-dive with infra for late April/early May.
[08:25] Sara: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:27] Alex: Thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
